# Overview

This vignette follows the basic workflow of
[Orchestrating Single-Cell Analysis with Bioconductor](https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA/)
(OSCA) on a real dataset, and clusters it with `clusterLibreville`: quality
control, normalisation, feature selection, PCA and UMAP as in OSCA, then
deterministic Leiden clustering, with a look at what determinism does and does
not buy.

```{r libraries}
library(clusterLibreville)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
```

Each step below names its package: quality control and normalisation from
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scuttle")`, pre-clustering for size factors, variance
modelling and PCA from `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scran")`, UMAP and plots from
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scater")`, graphs from `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("bluster")`.

# Data: mouse brain cells (Zeisel et al. 2015)

The Zeisel brain data (3005 cells), one of the datasets in
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("scRNAseq")`, comes with the authors' cell type labels,
so the clusters can be checked against them.

```{r data}
sce <- scRNAseq::ZeiselBrainData()
sce
table(sce$level1class)
```

# Preprocessing, as in OSCA

Quality control on library size, detected genes, mitochondrial and spike-in
proportions:

```{r qc}
is.mito <- grepl("^mt-", rownames(sce))
stats <- scuttle::perCellQCMetrics(sce, subsets = list(Mt = is.mito))
qc <- scuttle::quickPerCellQC(
    stats, percent_subsets = c("altexps_ERCC_percent", "subsets_Mt_percent"))
sce <- sce[, !qc$discard]
ncol(sce)
```

Normalisation by deconvolution, variance modelling and the top 10% of highly
variable genes, then PCA and UMAP. `scran::quickCluster()` is only a coarse
pre-clustering, so that `scran::computeSumFactors()` pools similar cells when
estimating size factors; it is not the clustering this vignette is about:

```{r normalise}
set.seed(1000)
clusters <- scran::quickCluster(sce)
sce <- scran::computeSumFactors(sce, cluster = clusters)
sce <- scuttle::logNormCounts(sce)
dec <- scran::modelGeneVar(sce)
hvg <- scran::getTopHVGs(dec, prop = 0.1)
set.seed(1001)
sce <- scran::fixedPCA(sce, rank = 50, subset.row = hvg)
set.seed(1002)
sce <- scater::runUMAP(sce, dimred = "PCA")
```

# Clustering

On a `SingleCellExperiment`, `leiden()` builds the shared nearest neighbour
graph of a reduced dimension (as `bluster::makeSNNGraph()` does) and returns
the labels as a factor, community 1 the largest:

```{r cluster}
colLabels(sce) <- leiden(sce, use.dimred = "PCA", k = 10, seed = 0)
table(colLabels(sce))
scater::plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP", colour_by = "label", text_by = "label")
```

The clusters against the published cell types:

```{r agreement}
table(cluster = colLabels(sce), type = sce$level1class)
bluster::pairwiseRand(colLabels(sce), sce$level1class, mode = "index")
```

At resolution 1 Leiden finds more clusters than there are published types.
Interneurons, astrocytes, endothelial-mural cells and microglia each map to one
cluster, while CA1 pyramidal cells and oligodendrocytes are split into several
subpopulations (the authors' finer `level2class` labels split them too), and one
smaller cluster mixes types. The adjusted Rand index counts every split
against the clustering, so it is low here although most clusters are pure; the
resolution scan below shows how it changes.

# Determinism, and what it does not fix

The same seed gives the same clusters at any number of threads, so a result
is reproducible on a laptop and on a many-core server:

```{r determinism}
identical(leiden(sce, seed = 0, threads = 1),
          leiden(sce, seed = 0, threads = 4))
```

Determinism makes each seed reproducible; it does not make the partition
seed-independent. Modularity has many near-equal optima, so different seeds
can still disagree on some cells:

```{r seeds}
runs <- lapply(0:4, function(s) leiden(sce, seed = s))
agree <- outer(seq_along(runs), seq_along(runs), Vectorize(function(a, b)
    bluster::pairwiseRand(runs[[a]], runs[[b]], mode = "index")))
round(agree, 3)
```

Because every run is reproducible and cheap, many seeds (or resolutions) can be
run and summarised, e.g. into a consensus or a per-cell stability score.

# Did it converge?

`details = TRUE` returns how the run ended: the iterations it took, whether the
last one changed nothing (a fixed point), why it stopped, and the modularity.
By default Leiden runs until an iteration changes nothing; with a fixed
`n_iterations` it may stop before:

```{r converged}
str(leiden(sce, seed = 0, details = TRUE)[-1])
str(leiden(sce, seed = 0, n_iterations = 1, details = TRUE)[-1])
```

# Resolution

Higher resolutions give more, smaller clusters:

```{r resolution}
res <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2)
by_res <- lapply(res, function(r) leiden(sce, resolution = r, seed = 0))
data.frame(resolution = res,
           clusters = vapply(by_res, nlevels, integer(1)),
           ARI = vapply(by_res, function(l) bluster::pairwiseRand(
               l, sce$level1class, mode = "index"), numeric(1)))
```

```{r resolution-umap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4}
plots <- lapply(c(1, 4), function(i) {
    sce$res <- by_res[[i]]
    r <- res[i]
    scater::plotReducedDim(sce, "UMAP", colour_by = "res") +
        ggplot2::ggtitle(paste("resolution", r))
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(plots)
```

# Inside bluster, and next to igraph

`cluster_libreville()` has igraph's community-function interface, so it plugs
into bluster's graph-based clustering:

```{r bluster}
param <- bluster::SNNGraphParam(k = 10, cluster.fun = cluster_libreville,
                                cluster.args = list(seed = 0))
by_bluster <- bluster::clusterRows(reducedDim(sce, "PCA"), param)
identical(as.integer(by_bluster), as.integer(colLabels(sce)))
```

On the same graph, igraph's own Leiden (single-threaded) for comparison; the
modularity of both partitions is computed the same way:

```{r igraph}
g <- bluster::makeSNNGraph(reducedDim(sce, "PCA"), k = 10, type = "rank")
ig <- igraph::cluster_leiden(g, objective_function = "modularity",
                             n_iterations = 10)
c(clusterLibreville = modularity(g, colLabels(sce)),
  igraph = modularity(g, igraph::membership(ig)))
```

# Compared with the usual Bioconductor choices

`scran::clusterCells()` (OSCA's entry point, now `bluster::clusterRows()`)
clusters the same SNN graph with walktrap by default. bluster's
`cluster.fun = "leiden"` passes no arguments to `igraph::cluster_leiden()`, so
igraph's defaults apply: the *CPM* objective at resolution 1 (not modularity)
and 2 iterations. Each choice on the same graph:

```{r compare}
choices <- list(
    "walktrap (OSCA default)" = function(g) igraph::cluster_walktrap(g),
    "igraph leiden, defaults (CPM)" = function(g) igraph::cluster_leiden(g),
    "igraph leiden, modularity, 2 iterations" = function(g)
        igraph::cluster_leiden(g, objective_function = "modularity"),
    "clusterLibreville, 2 iterations" = function(g)
        cluster_libreville(g, seed = 0, n_iterations = 2),
    "igraph leiden, modularity, converged" = function(g)
        igraph::cluster_leiden(g, objective_function = "modularity",
                               n_iterations = -1),
    "clusterLibreville, converged" = function(g)
        cluster_libreville(g, seed = 0))
run <- lapply(choices, function(f) {
    # clustering only, on the SNN graph built above; best of 3
    secs <- vapply(1:3, function(i) {
        set.seed(0)
        system.time(comm <<- f(g))[["elapsed"]]
    }, numeric(1))
    list(labels = factor(igraph::membership(comm)), seconds = min(secs))
})
labels <- lapply(run, `[[`, "labels")
ari <- function(a, b) bluster::pairwiseRand(a, b, mode = "index")
ref <- labels[["clusterLibreville, converged"]]
data.frame(clusters = vapply(labels, nlevels, integer(1)),
           ARI_types = vapply(labels, ari, numeric(1), b = sce$level1class),
           ARI_libreville = vapply(labels, ari, numeric(1), b = ref),
           modularity = vapply(labels, function(l) modularity(g, l),
                               numeric(1)),
           seconds = vapply(run, `[[`, numeric(1), "seconds"))
```

With the modularity objective, igraph's Leiden and `clusterLibreville` find
essentially the same partition, at 2 iterations (igraph's default) and run to
convergence (`n_iterations = -1`; igraph's R package converges, but
python-igraph up to 0.11.9 runs a single iteration for -1). Times are for the
clustering step alone, on the machine that built this vignette; igraph runs on
one thread and `clusterLibreville` on all cores. At 2 iterations the two take
about the same time; run to convergence, igraph is the faster on a graph this
small (`r ncol(sce)` cells). `clusterLibreville`'s advantage is reproducibility
at any number of threads, and speed on large graphs.

Leiden through bluster with its default
arguments optimises CPM instead and splits the data into many small clusters:
pass `objective_function = "modularity"` (or a CPM resolution suited to the
graph's weights) when using it. Walktrap is a different algorithm, with its own
trade-offs.
